The War in Ethiopia
1
Al Jazeera

Renewed fighting in Ethiopia's Tigray region raises fears of full-scale civil war

Fighting spread across Ethiopia's Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions from September 23-26, 2026, after a new seven-group rebel coalition, the Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, launched coordinated attacks on federal forces and seized airports at Axum, Shire and Mekelle, threatening the November 2022 Pretoria peace deal. Ethiopia's government said it had killed more than 270 rebel fighters, a toll that could not be independently verified, while roughly 750,000 people were already displaced before the new escalation. Jervin Naidoo, a senior political analyst at Oxford Economics Africa, said, “Since the end of the war… there have been consistent violations on both sides.” Analysts warned the country risked a return to civil war, which killed an estimated 600,000 people from 2020 to 2022.

Addis Standard

U.S. senators urge Rubio to act as Ethiopia conflict escalates

Six U.S. senators — Jeanne Shaheen, Cory Booker, Chris Coons, Jeff Merkley, Chris Van Hollen and Tim Kaine — pressed Secretary of State Marco Rubio on September 28, 2026, to push Ethiopia's federal government, the Tigray People's Liberation Front and allied armed groups back to mediation as the conflict spread into Tigray, Afar and Oromia. The senators faulted the administration for letting human-rights sanctions under Executive Order 14046 lapse and cited a drone strike that damaged U.S.-funded food aid meant for displaced civilians. “We are alarmed by the deteriorating security situation in Ethiopia,” they wrote, warning that “the stakes are too high to risk another conflict in an already volatile Horn of Africa.”

Addis Standard

At least 150,000 displaced in Afar as Tigray TV hit by drone

Addis Standard cited a humanitarian source estimating at least 150,000 people had been displaced in Ethiopia's Afar region by September 28, 2026, as Tigrayan-aligned fighters advanced and a drone strike hit the state broadcaster Tigrai TV's building in Mekelle a day earlier, knocking it off air. The station, suspended by federal authorities on September 21 and staffed by roughly 400 employees, had its facade blackened and windows blown out, though no casualties were immediately reported. Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, chief of the Ethiopian National Defense Force, said, “We are fighting forces that are organized and allied to serve the interests of external forces.” The surge in displacement has strained aid operations already stretched thin by Ethiopia's 2020-2022 war.

Ethiopian army claims capture of strategic town

Ethiopia's National Defense Force claimed on September 27, 2026, to have recaptured the town of Sekota in Amhara region from Tigrayan-aligned forces, part of a wider counteroffensive as fighting raged across Tigray, Amhara and Afar following the rebel alliance's push into the north. The claim came a day after coalition fighters seized the Afar town of Erebti, and amid separate reports that federal troops had also retaken Alamata further south. Army chief Field Marshal Birhanu Jula has separately accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of arming the rebel side. Specific casualty figures and an on-the-record commander's statement on the Sekota claim itself could not be independently confirmed.

The dueling claims came as casualties and displacement from the renewed fighting continued to climb across northern Ethiopia.

BBC

Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces?

As Ethiopia's federal forces battled a new seven-group insurgent coalition through late September 2026, BBC Africa examined why former rivals — the Tigray People's Liberation Front, the Amhara Fano National Movement, the Oromo Liberation Army and others — chose to join forces against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. TPLF Vice President Amanuel Assefa said of the pact, formed after more than a year of talks, “We just formed an alliance, we are collaborating with several groups and our objectives are to remove the regime and facilitating a transitional government.” Fano commander Zemene Kassie was named to chair the coalition, though analysts have questioned whether its loosely coordinated fighters can match the government's drone-equipped military.

Army plane crash death toll revised to 17

The death toll from the September 25 military plane crash in Kenge, Kwango province, was revised upward to 17 — 16 adults and an infant — after firefighters extinguished the wreckage, officials said September 26. Among the dead were Lieutenant General Joseph Mutombo, first president of the High Military Court, and army auditor general Lieutenant General Lucien-René Likulia. The aircraft, flying from Kikwit to Kinshasa, developed a technical fault and attempted an emergency landing with no runway available. “With no landing strip available in Kenge, the plane crashed into a residential plot,” said Kwango deputy governor Rémy Saki Bokinda. President Félix Tshisekedi ordered an investigation, and the transport ministry suspended the plane's operator, Tracep Congo Aviation.

At least 12 dead and dozens missing after another vessel capsizes in DRC

A vessel carrying more than 50 people capsized on Lake Kivu off Idjwi Island, South Kivu province, on the night of September 26, 2026, killing at least 12 people and leaving dozens missing, local officials said. About 15 people were rescued from the boat, which was transporting fish traders and goods between Bwina and Boza; the cause of the sinking was not immediately clear. “The vessel was carrying more than 50 people when it capsized on Saturday night in the Idjwi territory, in South Kivu province,” said Félix Habiragi, chief of Kisheke village. The accident came just two days after a separate capsizing on Lake Tanganyika killed at least 41 people, part of a pattern of deadly boat disasters on DRC's lakes.

Christian Science Monitor

Somaliland's women shoot high on and off the court

In Hargeisa, capital of the self-declared but unrecognized republic of Somaliland, women's basketball has grown since pioneer Khadra Mohamed Abdi began training girls from her home decades ago despite community opposition. Hafsa Omer, now in her mid-20s, founded the team Hiil Hableed — meaning female solidarity — eight years ago as a high schooler; it now draws more than 3,000 followers online. Players practice on a government court in Hargeisa reserved for men on other nights and march wrapped in Somaliland's flag during independence celebrations, using the sport to press for both gender equality and the diplomatic recognition Somaliland has sought since declaring independence from Somalia in 1991. “It is my role and responsibility to make sure the world sees me,” said player Nimo Ahmed.

Surge of refugees into Chad amid reports of rape and abductions

Daily refugee arrivals from Sudan into Chad surged twentyfold to more than 400 people a day, with over 55,000 crossing in 2026 and nearly 1 million since April 2023, the UN refugee agency reported on September 25, 2026. Most cross at the Adré and Tiné border points, fleeing clashes, airstrikes and drone attacks across Darfur, Kordofan and Blue Nile; women and girls described armed groups subjecting fleeing civilians to abduction, sexual assault and rape en route. A Tiné facility housing 4,300 people faces severe water and sanitation shortages, and roughly 190,000 refugees remain in informal border sites awaiting relocation. UN regional refugee coordinator Mamadou Dian Balde said “testimonies gathered from new arrivals underline the catastrophic human toll of the conflict.”

Judge imposes £100,000 bail condition on Rwanda genocide accused

A London judge set a £100,000 bail condition, reported September 28, 2026, for Vincent Brown, 65, formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, the first person charged in the UK over the 1994 Rwandan genocide. Judge Mark Lucraft KC at the Old Bailey ordered Brown to surrender his passport, submit to electronic monitoring, observe a curfew at his London home and report daily to police pending trial. Prosecutor Jane Stansfield told the court he was “a leader or supervisor of physical acts of violence which were carried out by others.” Brown denies the allegations and is due back in court October 9.

Middle East Eye reported that a TikTok video in August 2026 describing France's mountains as “exclusively reserved for white people” and free of “Wallah and Gucci caps” drew a wave of racist comments before going viral, prompting a counter-movement of Black and Muslim hikers asserting their right to the outdoors. One commenter told critics to “stay where you belong, in your Islamised districts,” while hiking organiser Zeynab Alabbar responded, “We love nature too.” A 2020 Grenoble study by researcher Lea Sallenave had already found hikers noticing that “the higher [they] climbed, the whiter the people [they] encountered seemed.” The debate comes as France's far-right National Rally, which leads 2027 presidential polls, pushes to ban hijabs in public spaces.

UAE behind some of Africa's worst wars

An Instagram post circulating in 2026 claimed the United Arab Emirates is behind some of Africa's worst wars, echoing years of documented reporting on Emirati involvement in the continent's conflicts. UN Panels of Experts and Amnesty International have accused the UAE of funnelling weapons, including Chinese- and British-made arms, to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces militia, while analysts have separately linked Emirati-connected gold networks to the M23 rebellion in eastern DR Congo. The UAE has repeatedly denied arming the RSF. Because the claim originated from an Instagram post rather than a news outlet, its specific wording should be treated cautiously unless independently corroborated by the reporting above.

Investigation reveals thousands of Africans recruited into Russian military

A Journalists for Justice investigation published on 26 September 2026 found that at least 3,066 Africans from 40 countries have been recruited into Russia's military since October 2022, with 502 confirmed killed in action by June 2026. Kenya topped the list with 873 documented recruits, ahead of Egypt (407), Cameroon (383) and Ghana (337), as fighters were lured into the war in Ukraine with promises of high pay. Kenya's National Assembly Majority Leader Kimani Ichung'wah said many recruits were “basically just given a gun to go and die,” describing an “organised transnational trafficking syndicate recruiting Kenyan citizens under false pretences.”

Half of Africa relies more on diesel generators than on the grid for power

Semafor reported on 28 September 2026 that roughly half of sub-Saharan African countries now rely more on diesel generators than on national grids for electricity, with diesel accounting for about 63% of the region's grid-connected generation capacity, excluding North Africa and South Africa. The report cited research finding at least 26 sub-Saharan markets where generator capacity now exceeds grid capacity, reflecting how persistent power shortfalls push businesses and households toward costly, import-dependent diesel as a coping mechanism. The shift leaves many economies exposed to volatile global fuel prices. The newsletter's full figures and analysis could not be independently confirmed through other sources; readers should treat the exact details as unverified pending direct access to the original piece.

Who are the candidates vying to lead La Francophonie?

The New Times reported that four candidates are competing to become the next Secretary-General of the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF), with member states set to vote at the 20th Francophonie Summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, in November 2026. The field includes incumbent Louise Mushikiwabo of Rwanda, Juliana Amato Lumumba of DR Congo, Coumba Bâ of Mauritania, and Romania's Dacian Cioloș, who pitched their visions to the 53 full member states at a public hearing in Paris in June. Mushikiwabo said, “Am I afraid of an election? No, I am not afraid of an election,” adding that “the decision will be made by the heads of state who will vote.” The winner serves a 2027-2030 term.

43The Guardian

Banished: the secret Trump deals sending migrants across the world

The Guardian's Banished investigation, published 28 September 2026, examined secret deals under which the Trump administration paid or pressured dozens of countries to accept migrants deported from the US who are not their own nationals. Reporters documented more than 25,000 people removed to third countries, including over 5,000 sent to nations across Africa, Latin America, the Caribbean and Central Asia, such as Ghana, Liberia, Eswatini and the Central African Republic, with Washington pledging at least $410 million to secure the agreements. Immigration lawyer Alma David described the removals bluntly: “These are people who were kidnapped, essentially.” A State Department spokesperson said the administration remained “unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration.”
